opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and it's something I've been thinking about a lot. For a long time in locomotion, we've treated the problem as almost purely geometric. The robot looks at the terrain, maybe builds a height map, and the policy figures out where to put its feet so it doesn't fall. That works really well outdoors on rocks, stairs, slopes, the kind of things we showed in a lot of the early legged robot work.

But an office is a very different environment. Geometrically it's actually pretty easy: flat floors, maybe some stairs. The hard part is that everything around you has meaning. A cable on the floor looks like a tiny bump, but you really shouldn't step on it. A chair might move if you push it. A glass door has almost no geometry in a depth sensor, but you definitely can't walk through it. And then there are people, who aren't obstacles in the normal sense. You need to keep a comfortable distance, not cut in front of someone, maybe slow down near them.

So if your policy only sees geometry, it can be perfectly stable and still behave badly. It walks over someone's laptop bag because it's technically traversable, or it treats a person like a pillar. To behave well you need to know what things are, not just where they are. That's where semantics comes in, and I think it's increasingly where vision-language models and larger pretrained representations come in too. You get that common-sense understanding of the world, and then the question becomes how to connect it to the low-level, high-frequency control that keeps the robot balanced. Bridging those two levels is, I think, one of the most interesting open problems right now.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts easy-to-traverse office floors with semantically meaningful items such as cables, glass doors, and laptop bags that the robot should avoid, explaining that it must identify what things are rather than rely only on geometry.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the easiest way to see it is to look at what a typical locomotion policy actually gets as input. For most of the work we did on ANYmal, and really most of the legged locomotion literature, the policy sees proprioception, so joint positions, velocities, the base orientation, and then some representation of the terrain, usually a height map or a depth image. That's a purely geometric view of the world. And that's fine when the world is a staircase or a rocky trail, because geometry is really all that matters there. A rock is something you step on, and the height tells you everything you need.

But in an office, geometry stops being enough. You have a chair, a cardboard box, a person's legs, a glass table, a cable on the floor. To a height map, a cardboard box and a step look basically identical. The policy will happily try to climb onto the box, which might collapse, or it will treat a person as an obstacle to step over. And things like a glass wall or a shiny floor break the depth sensors entirely, so the geometric estimate is just wrong.

So the question becomes, what should the robot do with an object, not just where is it. Can I step on this, should I avoid it, is it going to move, is it fragile. Those are semantic properties, and you cannot read them off the height field. And this is really where the recent progress in vision-language models gets interesting for us, because for the first time you have something that can give you a reasonable prior about what an object is and how to treat it, without having to hand-label every category.

The way I think about it is less that the low-level controller suddenly needs to understand language, and more that the locomotion skill has to be conditioned on information that comes from a semantic layer. The reactive part, balancing, foot placement, recovering from slips, stays fast and learned in simulation like before. But the decisions about where to put your feet, what to treat as traversable, how cautious to be, those should be informed by what the thing actually is. Otherwise you get a robot that is very athletic and very dumb, and in a space shared with people that's not a good combination.

r001.rationale: The response says semantic information helps determine what is traversable and whether to step on or avoid an object, distinguishing safe surfaces from objects such as fragile boxes or people.

astra-6.text:
Well, in an office, geometry alone doesn’t tell you where you should step. You might have a cable on the floor, or someone’s bag, or a sheet of paper. Physically, the robot might be able to walk over all of those, but that doesn’t mean it should. You want it to understand something about what those objects are and how to behave around them.

So semantics gives the locomotion policy context beyond whether a surface can support a foot or whether an obstacle is small enough to cross. It helps the robot choose movements that are appropriate for a space shared with people, rather than just movements that keep it from falling.

r001.rationale: The response says geometry may show that a robot can walk over a cable, bag, or paper, while semantics helps it understand what those objects are and decide how to behave around them.

sol-6.1.text:
Because getting around an office isn’t just about finding a surface you can physically step on. A policy might see a desk as a flat, stable surface, but we don’t want the robot to walk across it. And a person isn’t simply an obstacle—you want to give them space and behave predictably around them.

So semantics helps connect what the robot can do physically with what it should do in that environment. The locomotion policy needs some understanding of what things are, or guidance from a system that has that understanding, to choose appropriate behavior.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts a physically walkable desk that the robot should avoid with people it should give space to, explaining that semantics helps it choose appropriate behavior based on what things are.
